Miller and colleagues treat the same estimation problem, a failure probability from testing that revealed no failure, and treat explicitly input distributions other than the uniform one [@miller1992nofailures].

Reliability growth is the second idea. As bugs are found and fixed, the rate at which testing finds new ones falls, and a model of that fall predicts how many bugs remain. Goel and Okumoto modeled software failures as a non-homogeneous Poisson process whose rate of detection changes with testing time [@goel1979nhpp], and several models of the same family followed. Each assumes a stationary test process: the same kind of testing, applied at a steady rate, to a design whose only changes are the fixes. The assumptions are this chapter's, at the scale of a project, and they break in the same ways: a new generator, a new test, a new feature.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
Malka and Ziv, at IBM in 1998, fitted reliability-growth models to the bug history of two superscalar PowerPC processor projects: bugs found by random simulation, counted against cumulative simulated cycles, with bugs found by other means left out [@malka1998bugdata]. They checked for growth with the Laplace trend test before fitting, and compared three models. For processor A, a model fitted three months before the end of the project predicted about 790 bugs in total, against 794 found. For processor B, a feature added in the middle of the project broke the trend, and only the data after it could be fitted. Their own caveats are part of the result: no one model was clearly better than the others, and the predictions describe the test environment, not the design's behavior in the field. It is the one published application of these statistics to a real hardware project found in writing this chapter, and it is dated: a regression of 1998 and one of today differ in more than size.
:::

Two limits apply to any such curve. Butler and Finelli argue that reliability-growth models do not escape the scale problem of @sec-ch21-clean: showing a very small failure rate still takes testing on the order of the reciprocal of the rate [@butler1993infeasibility]. And a falling bug rate says the current generator is running out of bugs it can reach, which is the discovery probability of @sec-ch21-unseen at the scale of a project, with the same Pitfall attached. Böhme and Paul give the quantitative case for the usual remedy, random testing first and directed tests for the holes: in their model a systematic strategy beats random testing only if each systematic test costs less than a bound set mainly by the confidence wanted, about four random tests' worth at 90% and more at higher confidence, and a strategy that starts random and switches to systematic does as well as the better of the two [@boehme2016efficiency]. A reader handed a growth curve as evidence of readiness can ask four questions of it: what generator and what checkers produced the bugs, whether either changed during the period fitted, whether the design changed in anything but fixes, and whether a trend test was run before a model was fitted. A curve that survives all four is a statement about the test process, as Malka and Ziv say of their own. Bug-rate curves as a sign-off metric belong to a later chapter, Metrics, Closure and Sign-off.

## Worked example: sizing and signing off the FIFO regression {#sec-ch21-example}

The sections above, run in the order an engineer would run them, make one loop: estimate the rates, size the regression, run it, check what it did not reach, check that the stimulus is what was asked for, and write down what the clean seeds prove. The example `worked` does all six on the FIFO, with the testbench of @sec-ch08-example and the RTL of @sec-ch01 read by path, and the checking testbench of @sec-ch09-example for the last step. Its runner shows the order; the size of the second run is not typed in but computed from the first:

```{.bash include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run_worked.sh" lines="14-22"}
```

**Step 1, the pilot.** Two hundred seeds of the even-odds 200-cycle generator, numbered from 5001 so that they share nothing with the seeds of the earlier sections, give a per-seed rate for every bin with its interval:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="1-16"}
```

The ranking matches the thousand-seed run of @sec-ch21-p, with wider intervals: the four full cells near a fifth, `full` and `almost` near a quarter, and `full_16` never hit, as the exclusion review of @sec-ch08-example says it cannot be.

**Step 2, the size.** The union bound of @sec-ch21-coupon over every bin the pilot reached, at 99%:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="17-25"}
```

Thirty-two seeds, and the bound says why: the four cells of `op_x_full` contribute 95% of the remaining risk at that size. Those are the bins a better test would target, and if the regression is too slow these are where a reweighting would pay. The pilot's rates are a little lower than the thousand-seed run's, so the answer is larger than the 27 of @sec-ch21-coupon; a bound computed from a pilot inherits the pilot's sampling error, and a more cautious sizing would use the lower ends of the intervals.

**Step 3, the run.** Thirty-two fresh seeds, from 6001, merged into one database with `verilator_coverage --write`:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="26-29"}
```

Every bin the pilot reached is hit, and the one bin at zero is the excluded one. The covergroup is closed, and the union bound said in advance that it would be with probability at least 0.99, if the pilot's rates are right.

**Step 4, the unseen.** Chao2 and Good-Turing over the 32 seeds of the run:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="30-32"}
```

No bin was seen in only one or two seeds, so neither estimator indicates a reachable bin left to find. That is a statement about this generator, and @sec-ch21-unseen showed that it can hold while bins are missing; here, the exclusion review and the estimate agree, and the 30-cycle counter-example is the reason to check both.

**Step 5, the stimulus.** The driver draws an operation every cycle with each of the four operations at a quarter, and `op_cp` has already counted them. A chi-square test on data the covergroup collected anyway:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="33-35"}
```

The operation is drawn afresh each cycle and its bin depends on nothing else, so this is the case of @sec-ch21-seed in which cycles are independent draws, and the test is valid at the cycle level. The counts are consistent with the asked law, $p = 0.74$.

**Step 6, the sentence.** The covergroup measures stimulus and checks nothing, so the clean-seed bound needs a checker. The temporal-properties chapter's checking testbench, with its assertions bound to the design, runs 400 cycles of random traffic that fills the FIFO for 200 cycles and drains it for 200. It runs under 1000 seeds on the repaired FIFO of @sec-ch09-example, and, as the control, under the same seeds on the original:

```{.text include="examples/ch21-statistics-random-testing/worked/run.out" lines="36-46"}
```

On the repaired FIFO all 1000 seeds are clean, and the bound is 0.0030, the rule of three's $3/1000$. On the original all 1000 fail, and the chain says why: under this traffic a seed reaches fifteen entries, where the original raises `full` too early and the checker objects, with probability 1.000000. A checker that can fail, a generator that reaches the bug, and a bound on the repaired design: the three together are what make the sentence worth printing. The qualifier repeats @sec-ch21-clean: the 30-cycle generator would have produced 250 clean seeds on the original FIFO with probability 0.98. The repair also changes the meaning of the covergroup: on the repaired FIFO `full_16` becomes reachable and `almost` no longer means full, so the bin list and its exclusions are a property of the RTL, which is the "RTL unchanged" condition of @sec-ch21-clean in miniature.

Every step can fail, and each failure has a different remedy. A bin with no hits in the pilot is not sized at all: it goes to the exclusion review if it cannot be reached and to a new test or a reweighted constraint if it can. A fresh run that leaves a reached bin at zero is the one outcome in a hundred the bound allows, or a sign that the pilot's rates were optimistic; rerun the pilot larger, or size from the lower ends of its intervals. A Chao2 estimate above the seen count says the generator has more to give, and Good-Turing says how much one more seed is worth. A rejected histogram is a finding about the solver or the testbench, and @sec-ch21-uniform says to confirm it with a larger sample before acting. And a checker that cannot fail on the original design makes the clean-seed bound worthless, which is why the control run on the original is part of step 6 and not an extra.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example"}
Sizing and signing off a random regression. (1) Run a pilot of a few hundred seeds of the generator as it will be used, and read every bin's per-seed hit rate, with its interval, from the coverage databases. (2) Compute the smallest $n$ with $\sum_i (1-p_i)^n \le \delta$ over the bins the pilot reached, and list the bins that carry most of the sum; a bin with no hits goes to the exclusion review or to a new test, not into the formula. (3) Run $n$ fresh seeds, merge their databases, and confirm that every reached bin is hit. (4) Compute Chao2 and Good-Turing over the run, and read them as statements about this generator. (5) Test every histogram the run already holds against the law its constraint asks for, corrected for the number of tests, at the unit where its draws are independent. (6) Run the checking testbench on the RTL being released, count the clean seeds, and write the bound with its qualifier: under this generator, on this RTL, with these checkers.
:::

## Future directions {#sec-ch21-future}

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
Four directions are visible from this chapter, and it claims no result for any of them. Near-uniform samplers give a guarantee within a stated tolerance of the uniform law [@chakraborty2015unigen2]; the distance between the model a solver happens to return and a draw within such a tolerance is what @sec-ch07-solver measured, and the power table of @sec-ch21-uniform says how large a sample a regression would need to tell the two apart. The estimators of @sec-ch21-unseen assume a generator that does not adapt; Böhme, Liyanage and Wüstholz's work on residual risk under adaptive fuzzing points toward estimators that hold when it does [@boehme2021residual], and a coverage-steered regression is the hardware case that needs them. Machine-learned closure flows are the case in which every estimator here loses its stationarity at once; Kwon and colleagues report such a flow for interconnect coverage, a report co-authored by the vendor of the tools it ran on and to be read as a vendor claim [@kwon-dvcon-simai]. And the `solve...before` result of @sec-ch21-uniform is a measurement of release 5.052; a later release lists a change to that feature [@verilator-changes], which this chapter has not measured.
:::

## Summary {#sec-ch21-summary}

- One object carries the chapter: the hit-probability vector $p$, the chance that one seeded run of a fixed generator on a fixed design hits each bin. Bins, bug triggers, cross cells and configuration tuples are entries of it, and every answer holds only for the generator that defined it.
- One bin needs $\ln\delta / \ln(1-p)$ tests, about $4.6/p$ for 99%. The FIFO's bug trigger, 247 of 1000 seeds, agrees with an exact Markov chain's 0.242. A cross cell's per-seed probability is joint: 0.187 for `push_x_full` against 0.271 for the product of its marginals.
- The seed, not the cycle, is the independent draw in a stateful design. A model of independent cycles predicted that 89.8% of seeds hit `almost`, where 27.1% did, and that 11 seeds close `fifo_cg`, where 25 are needed.
- The union bound $\sum_i (1-p_i)^n \le \delta$ needs no independence between bins and never under-states: 27 seeds for `fifo_cg` at 99%, against 25 measured. The rarest bins set the answer almost alone, and an unreachable bin makes it infinite.
- After $N$ clean seeds, the per-seed failure probability under this generator is below $3/N$ at 95%. The bound describes the generator, not the design: 250 clean seeds of a 30-cycle generator bounded the FIFO bug's rate by 0.0119 when the truth was $8.45 \times 10^{-5}$.
- A `dist` is a testable hypothesis. On release 5.052 every constraint shape tested held its law except `solve...before`, rejected at $p$ below $10^{-300}$. A non-rejection is a statement at a stated power, and many tests at once need a correction.
- A covering array makes configuration coverage small and deterministic: 23 rows for every legal pair of the DMA's transfer space, where uniform random selection needed a median of 200, and the DMA's own generator never reaches `max` at all. The stimulus inside each configuration is still random.
- Species estimators give lower bounds on the bins a generator will reach. Under the 30-cycle generator Chao2 and Good-Turing saw nothing missing while six reachable bins were unseen: a small discovery probability is not few missing bins.
- Entropy measures spread, KL divergence and $G$ measure distance from a law, and mutual information ranks which knob moves which bin; on the FIFO the most even generator was neither the one that reached most bins nor the one that found the bug. None of them measures checking.
- Reliability-growth models assume a stationary test process; a new generator, a new feature or a new RTL drop restarts the fit.

## Exercises {#sec-ch21-exercises}

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
1. A bin is hit by 1% of seeds. How many seeds give a 95% chance of hitting it at least once?
2. A regression ran 600 seeds, all clean. Give the exact one-sided 95% upper bound on the per-seed failure probability under that generator, and the value the rule of three gives.
3. Treat a fair six-sided die as a generator of six equally likely bins. What is the expected number of throws until every face has been seen?
4. A covergroup has 28 reachable bins, and the rarest is hit by 18.7% of seeds. Taking every one of the 28 bins at that rarest rate, and using the union bound with the risk split equally among the bins, how many seeds guarantee that every bin is hit with probability at least 0.99?
5. The packet stream of @sec-ch07-example draws kind 2 with weight 1 in 10 for every packet. What is the probability that a 64-packet run contains no packet of kind 2?
6. A bin is hit in 1.13% of the cycles of 200-cycle seeds. (a) What fraction of seeds does a model of independent cycles predict will hit it? (b) The measured fraction is 0.27. Using the measured fraction, how many seeds give a 99% chance of a hit?
7. After ten seeds, 60 bins have been seen; 4 of them were seen in exactly one seed and 2 in exactly two. Compute Chao2.
8. After 200 seeds, three bins have been seen in exactly one seed each. What is the Good-Turing estimate of the number of new bins the next seed will show, which is also an upper estimate of the chance that it shows any?
9. A histogram of 10,000 draws has counts 6076, 2940 and 984 against a 6:3:1 law. Compute Pearson's $X^2$, and decide at level 0.05, given that the critical value for 2 degrees of freedom is 5.99.
10. Give the entropy of the 6:3:1 law in bits, and its effective number of values.
11. A configuration space has factors with 6, 4, 3, 3 and 2 levels. By the trivial bound, what is the smallest number of tests any pairwise covering array of it can have?
12. Twenty binary configuration knobs are to be covered pairwise. By the formula of Kleitman and Spencer, what is the smallest covering array?
:::
